html:
The Aikanã are a small Indigenous people of Rondônia in western Brazil, near the border with Bolivia. Their language, also called Aikanã, is an isolate: it has no known relatives. Outsiders once called them Massacá or Tubarão.

Their region was opened up in the early 1900s by rubber tapping during the rubber boom and by the telegraph line of Cândido Rondon, who gave the state its name. Epidemics and loss of land followed. Today most Aikanã live on a reserve they share with the Kwazá and Latundê, two other small peoples. The Makurap live nearby in the same state.
